initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve distinct substantive works have actual-content inspection records: community publications from Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Eastern Shoshone and the Northwestern Band; a community–NPS exhibit; two place-based NPS histories; a Northwestern Shoshone historian’s selected chapter pages; a cited Wyoming history article; primary treaty and constitutional texts; and a federal Duck Valley water-settlement statement. These support a carefully scoped introduction across several regional communities, but the entry is a broad umbrella and evidence depth remains uneven. Reaching the source target does not make the collection complete or community-reviewed.
remainingLimits: The entry’s broad “Shoshone” access point cannot stand in for separate studies of the many Shoshone governments, communities, bands, and family histories. The current sample is uneven across Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, the Northwestern Band, and other Shoshone communities.

More community-authored histories, language materials, and contemporary accounts from Shoshone governments in Nevada, Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming remain to be inspected; no single source represents all communities.

The Fort Bridger Treaty text, the Shoshone-Bannock Treaty Day account, and WyoHistory describe the separate Bannock reservation and later move using different chronology. The relationship between reservation promises, relocation, and later Fort Hall governance needs further original-record review.

Mae Parry’s 2000 chapter was reviewed at selected pages only. Its family and oral-history evidence is attributed, while its historical interpretations are not treated as universal community consensus.

The Shoshone-Paiute cultural page and Eastern Shoshone About page contain undated or broad totals and historical claims that require independent checking; no current population, acreage, or deep-time claim is reused.

The Shoshone-Bannock and Shoshone-Paiute language evidence here is introductory. Comparative specialist work on Shoshone varieties, Bannock, and Northern Paiute, with each community’s terminology and stewardship preferences, remains needed.
No community review or endorsement is recorded. No historical map was independently inspected for this batch and none has been newly assigned.

name: Tonkawa

initialAdequacy.rationale: Twelve substantive inspected works support a careful initial guide: the Tribe’s public history and language materials, TxDOT’s 2021 historical synthesis, Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study, the 1837 Texas treaty, the 1846 multination Council Springs treaty, the 1891 federal agreement record, a council-adopted Tonkawa memorial with member affidavits, the corrected Fifth Circuit opinion on the 1866 Texas act, a scholarly study of the 1862 massacre, an 1866 Texas governor’s letter, and an 1876 federal compilation on Tonkawa and Lipan people at Fort Griffin. Five supporting access/context references remain excluded. The new congressional document adds government correspondence about ration decisions and proposed relocation; it is not Tonkawa testimony and does not show that proposals were implemented. The collection still relies heavily on government and outside written records and does not provide a full Tonkawa-authored account of the massacre. It remains unfinished and does not settle the causes of the 1862 attack, consent to the 1891 cession, or all questions about historical Texas relationships.
remainingLimits: The 1862 massacre article is a secondary interpretation. Tonkawa-authored or community-held public accounts of the event and the original underlying government records need further review; no single-cause explanation is adopted.
The timing/direction of earlier movement, composition of named bands, language classification, and archaeological associations remain contested or uncertain.

The 1837 treaty, 1891 agreement, and 1907 memorial have been read, but related federal/Republic records, ratification/implementation documentation, and later claim disposition still require systematic review.
The 1846 Council Springs treaty scan’s transcribed text and signatory pages were read; separate ratification instruments, later implementation, and Tonkawa-specific interpretations remain unreviewed.

Current community-authored cultural, language-program, and historical publications need broader review. The 2020 museum booklet and large dictionary were not fully inspected; failed automated access is not treated as a paywall.
The documentary site describes collaboration and an oral-history film project, but neither film nor interviews were viewed; culturally sensitive footage may require limits on public use.
Current population, enrollment, acreage, and program-status figures are not claimed from undated pages.
This review did not inspect or add maps.

name: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo

initialAdequacy.rationale: Eight substantive inspected works provide a clearly bounded introduction grounded in the Pueblo’s own history and recent reporting, community-directed planning material, the 1987 law and committee report, and two Park Service accounts of the related Isleta/Ysleta landscape. The TxDOT report adds a broad historical and cultural-landscape synthesis with documented review by the Pueblo’s Department of Cultural Preservation; its source content and purpose are described clearly, and culturally sensitive location details were excluded. This evidence supports basic identification, a cautiously attributed movement history, settlement, legal framework, governance, and publicly documented language/cultural work. The source set remains an adequate starting guide, not a full deep dive, current legal opinion, comprehensive linguistic study, or community-reviewed account.
remainingLimits: Further Pueblo-authored and community-controlled public historical scholarship is needed; the 2016 report and 2025 annual report each have limited purposes, and TxDOT’s consulted synthesis does not replace a Pueblo-authored monograph.
Primary Spanish records and additional independent scholarship are needed to compare the chronology, route, and differing historical counts associated with movement to Ysleta.
Current language documentation and later legal developments have not been reviewed; program descriptions and the 1987 statute are not substitutes.
No community review or endorsement is recorded, and protected digital archive materials were not accessed.

remainingGaps: Read further Pueblo-authored historical essays and publicly released educational material, while respecting community-controlled archival access.

Compare the Pueblo’s oral-history framing with relevant Spanish-language colonial records and independent historical scholarship; preserve disagreement over the chronology and number of people who moved south.
Locate and inspect the Pueblo’s own language publications or approved learning resources. The 2025 annual report describes classes, not the language’s grammar, local variety, or current fluency.
Review later federal laws, court opinions, and current Pueblo legal materials before making claims about present jurisdiction, land status, or implementation of the 1987 Act.

The 2016 socioeconomic study is a dated community planning snapshot. Present-day member distribution and demographics have not been independently established; undated membership totals on Pueblo webpages conflict and are not repeated.
The Cultural Center lists some programming for Tribal Members only. No private archive, sensitive site, ceremonial detail, or community review is included in this public guide.
